newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Russian troops under fire in Tajikistan.
newsitem.headline: Russian troops under fire in Tajikistan.

text.p: A spate of recent attacks against Russian peacekeepers in the former Soviet republic of Tajikistan has come as the government and its Islamist opponents prepare for delicate talks in Tehran aimed at ending a bloody civil war.

On Saturday, Alexei Sarychev, a warrant officer with Russia's 201st Motorised Infantry Division, died and four of his comrades were wounded when their car exploded after a shopping trip to the main market in the capital, Dushanbe.
The attack was the fifth against the division in just over a week. The bodies of other victims were found on the street, killed in the night by anonymous attackers armed with Russian Makarov pistols.
No group has claimed responsibility for the killings and Russian military officials have so far drawn a blank as to who the "unidentified terrorists" might be.
About 20,000 Russian soldiers carry out peacekeeping duties in the republic, torn apart by a four-year civil war, and guard its remote, mountainous frontier with Afghanistan.

Diplomats and the Russian military have in the past pointed fingers at Tajikistan's Islamist opposition which has waged a guerrilla war against the secular government from the Pamir mountains and out of bases across the Afghan border.

Russian troops in Tajikistan -- cut off from Russia by more than 1,000 km (miles) of Kazakh territory -- see themselves as a bulwark against militant Islam on Russia's vulnerable southern flank after the loss of territory which followed the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991.
"I was told by one (Russian) commander that any Moslem is a terrorist," one Western diplomat in Dushanbe told Reuters.
"They think they're the last bastion against marauding Islamic forces from the south."
The Kremlin has also viewed the rise of the radical Islamic Taleban militia in Afghanistan with alarm.
Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov's shaky administration is heavily reliant on the Russian military for its tenuous grip on the impoverished republic of 5.7 million.

Opposition fighters already hold around half of the country, albeit sparsely populated mountain areas. Foreign United Nations military observers have been harassed by various armed groups, including Tajik troops, amid the general lawlessness.
Russian servicemen are driven to and from work accompanied by armed escorts. Vehicles carrying Russian soldiers have been hit with rocket-propelled grenades in the centre of Dushanbe.

Like the French in Algeria during the war of independence in the 1950s, Russians in uniform are easy targets for the unknown assailants who strike with impunity and melt back into the poorly lit streets and crowded bazaars of the Tajik capital.

But while the identity of the attackers remains unclear, the Russian military and diplomats are certain their motive is to smash a fragile peace agreed between the government and the opposition in Moscow last month.

"Determined destructive forces are preparing a savage attack which, if it will not destroy, will at least put in doubt the implementation of the accords," said a statement from the peacekeeping forces, quoted by Russia's Interfax news agency.
Observers point to a pattern of recurring violence in Tajikistan whenever the warring sides prepare to strengthen their hand at the negotiating table.
A ceasefire appears to be staving off any head-on clash.
But the violence has rekindled fears of renewed fighting as the warring sides prepare to resume delicate talks on power-sharing in the Iranian capital Tehran on Monday.
